commands.review_summary:
This PR makes Telegram client-options cache entries retain and retire their owned transports, defers closure until active operation and request leases drain, and adds regression coverage for eviction, retries, pre-request work, and Promise rejection contracts.

PR surface: Source +336, Tests +406. Total +742 across 3 files.

Reproducibility: yes. Current main creates an owned transport, caches only the derived client options, and evicts the entry without closing the transport; the PR's 65-key production-mode churn scenario exercises that source-visible leak.

target.title: fix(telegram): long-running sends leak connections after cache evictions
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where long-running Telegram senders could keep abandoned HTTP transports alive when the Telegram client options cache evicted old account/network entries.

## Why This Change Was Made

The cache entry now retains the transport created for its client fetch so eviction can release the old dispatcher lifecycle instead of only deleting the client options object. Evicted entries are retired immediately, but their transport is closed only after active Telegram request or operation leases finish, including retry waits and pre-first-request media preparation, so cache pressure does not abort an in-flight, retrying, or still-preparing Telegram send.

## User Impact

Operators running Telegram channels with many account or network option combinations should see stale Telegram transports released after cache eviction instead of accumulating idle connections over time, without changing existing Telegram send behavior for active requests.

## Evidence

- Live/near-real proof passed with a local Telegram Bot API substitute and the real `sendMessageTelegram` entry point. The refreshed run sent through 65 distinct production-mode account cache entries, observed 65 HTTP `POST /bot.../sendMessage` requests, and observed 6 undici dispatcher `destroy()` calls after cache eviction.
- Focused Telegram proxy regression passed: 1 file passed, 11 tests passed. The regressions drive 65 production-mode cache entries, verify the evicted transport `close()` is called, verify eviction defers `close()` until the active send finishes, verify eviction waits while a retryable send is sleeping between attempts, verify eviction also waits while media is loading before the first Telegram API request, verify eviction waits while a reaction helper persists a resolved target before its first action request, and verify injected Telegram API callers do not allocate an unused cached transport.
- The complete Telegram send test file passed: 1 file passed, 167 tests passed. Added coverage verifies all 12 exported Promise APIs report context setup failures as Promise rejections, and verifies invalid sticker/forum-topic inputs are rejected before constructing a Telegram client.
- The Promise boundary impact sweep confirmed the runtime re-exports and `Promise<T>` signatures are unchanged, production consumers await or forward the returned Promise, `typeof`-based test doubles remain compatible, and no caller relies on synchronous throws.
- Extensions type checking passed with `pnpm tsgo:test:extensions`.
- `OPENCLAW_DEV_AUTO_PAIR=false start_openclaw_dev_gateway.sh` — isolated OpenClaw dev gateway reached ready; the startup log recorded `http server listening` and `ready`.

Before the fix, the eviction regression failed with `expected "vi.fn()" to be called 1 times, but got 0 times` for the evicted transport close spy. Before the retry-window, media-load, and sibling-helper lease fixes, the focused regressions failed because the evicted transport closed while a retryable send was waiting between attempts, while a media send was still loading before the first Telegram API request, and while a reaction helper was still persisting a resolved target before its first action request. Before the Promise-contract follow-up, all 12 context-failure cases threw synchronously and three invalid-input cases constructed a Telegram client before rejecting. The regressions cover both the active-operation lease boundaries and the public Promise/validation-order contracts.
